analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set enforceable drinking water limits for toxic PFAS chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate committee vote or floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to set a national, enforceable limit on PFAS — man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, and firefighting foam — in public drinking water, within two years, covering at least PFOA and PFOS. It would have required the limits to protect people at higher risk, such as children and pregnant women, and prioritized federal help for small, rural, and disadvantaged water systems that face the biggest costs to comply. Introduced by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand with Senators Warren and Feinstein, it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of Americans whose drinking water contains PFAS. Communities near military bases, airports, and industrial sites where PFAS-contaminated firefighting foam and wastewater have leached into groundwater would get a federal ceiling on exposure, and people at elevated risk — including children — would be specifically protected. Small and rural water systems would get priority technical assistance and funding to comply.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish a maximum contaminant level and a national drinking water regulation for PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, within two years of enactment.
Requires the regulation to be protective of the health of subpopulations at greater risk from PFAS exposure than the general population.
Directs the EPA to prioritize technical assistance and funding to help small, rural, or disadvantaged public water systems comply with the new limits.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that made or used PFOA and PFOS, and water utilities that would have to test for and filter PFAS out of their supplies. Compliance costs would be passed to water ratepayers, which is why the bill directs aid to small and rural systems.

drawbacks.text: Setting a strict national limit would impose real treatment and monitoring costs on water utilities, and those costs would ultimately flow to ratepayers — the bill addresses this only partially, through voluntary prioritization of assistance for small and rural systems rather than dedicated funding.

Supporters of a slower approach argue that PFAS is a broad class of thousands of chemicals and that regulating it by class, using extrapolation tools like GenRA as the bill allows, could set limits before the science on individual chemicals is settled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — an enforceable federal ceiling on a toxic chemical in drinking water — is concrete and long-lasting; unlike most water rules, the costs fall partly on the polluting industry and partly on utilities that did not create the contamination. The main honest objection is the compliance bill for utilities and ratepayers, which the bill softens for small systems but does not fully fund.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on July 21, 2021, joined by Senators Warren and Feinstein.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — the last action ever taken on the bill.
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers that produced PFOA and PFOS and water systems that would have faced treatment and monitoring costs are better off, since no enforceable federal limit was imposed during this Congress. People exposed to PFAS in their drinking water got no federal protection from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat — Gillibrand plus 4 of the Senate's 48 Democrats, with no Republican support listed — and the bill never advanced past the committee.

industries.note: A national enforceable limit on PFOA and PFOS in drinking water would tighten regulation of the chemicals and increase liability pressure on the companies that made them. The bill's death left them facing no new federal drinking water standard from this Congress.

Utilities would bear testing and filtration costs to meet the new limits, but the bill prioritizes federal technical assistance and funding for small, rural, and disadvantaged systems. Utilities have no interest in the contamination itself; their cost is the bill's main cost to pass through to ratepayers.
